title: MP45-18 MISINFORMATION ON TIKTOK ABOUT THE EFFECT OF COVID-19 INFECTIONS AND VACCINATIONS ON MALE FERTILITY
screen_reason: Conference-abstract content analysis of 58 TikTok videos retrieved with #covidvaccine and #malefertility (1 Jan - 31 Dec 2021), reviewed by five independent researchers who coded the belief each video held. 6.9% of videos held the belief that the vaccine causes male infertility - a claim the abstract itself states is contradicted by the evidence ('the vaccine is not [associated with decreased sperm counts and quality]'). That is a share of items in a sample coded as endorsing a false claim, with a stated denominator, so CONTENT. Modified DISCERN is also reported and is kept as a QUALITY row (excluded from prevalence).

estimates.country: Not stated (TikTok videos retrieved by hashtag; the coding recorded presence of a 'US certified medical professional', and the authors are US-based)
estimates.measure_type: % of TikTok videos expressing the belief that the COVID-19 vaccine is responsible for male infertility
estimates.value_raw: 6.9% of 58 videos [the abstract states the percentage only; no count is given, 6.9% x 58 = 4]
estimates.denominator: 58 TikTok videos identified with the terms #covidvaccine and #malefertility between 1 January and 31 December 2021, after excluding unrelated videos
estimates.definition: The video was coded as holding the belief that the COVID-19 vaccine was responsible for male infertility - a claim the abstract states is contrary to the evidence.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Despite evidence about the lack of association between the COVID-19 vaccine and male fertility, social media platforms, including TikTok, continue to spread misleading information."
estimates.source_quote: Few videos believed that the vaccine was responsible for male infertility (6.9%).
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, RESULTS (J Urol 209, Suppl. 4, p. e628)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: "Videos were reviewed by five independent researchers" who recorded, among other items, the 'belief held on COVID-19 vaccine, infection and infertility'. No inter-rater reliability statistic, no adjudication rule and no external fact-check reference are reported in the abstract.
estimates.moderator_quote: After excluding unrelated videos, 58 videos using the terms #covidvaccine and #malefertility were identified on Tiktok from January 1 to December 31, 2021. Videos were reviewed by five independent researchers.
estimates.notes: Abstract-only source: no methods section, no reliability statistics, no country or search-date detail, and no statement of how many videos the hashtag search returned before the 'unrelated' exclusion. 4/58 = 6.897%, consistent with the verbatim 6.9%. denom_scope=topical (single-issue hashtag corpus on COVID vaccine and male fertility); denom_selection left empty because no rank truncation or top-N selection is described - though a hashtag search on TikTok is in practice relevance-ranked, which the abstract does not address. confidence=medium because the value and denominator are unambiguous but the coding procedure is undocumented.

estimates.country: Not stated (TikTok videos retrieved by hashtag)
estimates.measure_type: Mean modified DISCERN reliability score of the 58 videos (1 = poor to 5 = excellent)
estimates.value_raw: The average DISCERN score for the 58 videos was 2.93
estimates.denominator: 58 TikTok videos identified with #covidvaccine and #malefertility, 1 January - 31 December 2021
estimates.definition: Modified DISCERN reliability score, ranked from 1 = poor to 5 = excellent, applied to each video and averaged.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Despite evidence about the lack of association between the COVID-19 vaccine and male fertility, social media platforms, including TikTok, continue to spread misleading information."
estimates.source_quote: The average DISCERN score for the 58 videos was 2.93, PEMAT Understandability score was 76.1%, and PEMAT Actionability score was 25.7%.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, RESULTS (J Urol 209, Suppl. 4, p. e628)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Five independent researchers scored each video on the modified DISCERN reliability instrument; no inter-rater reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Information collected included video publication date, length, views, likes, comments, presence of US certified medical professional, demographic details, scientific article cited, belief held on COVID-19 vaccine, infection and infertility, modified DISCERN score and Patient Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT). The PEMAT score evaluated 17 items regarding understandability and actionability. The modified DISCERN based reliability score ranked quality from 1=poor, to 5=excellent.
estimates.notes: Kept as a QUALITY row per the protocol (DISCERN/GQS/JAMA scores are recorded but excluded from prevalence). It is a mean scale score, not a share, so value_kind=scale_score and value_pct carries the score itself (2.93 on a 1-5 scale), not a percentage.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED, with reasons: (1) 'Most videos were of the opinion that the COVID-19 infection causes infertility in men (48.3%)' - by the abstract's own framing this belief is broadly consistent with the evidence ('COVID-19 disease can be associated with decreased sperm counts and quality'), so it is not a misinformation share. (2) 37.9% held that the vaccine does NOT cause infertility - an accurate belief. (3) 67.2% of videos featured a medical professional - an author descriptor. (4) PEMAT Understandability 76.1% and Actionability 25.7% are quality-instrument scores expressed as percentages of instrument items, not shares of misinformation; I kept only one QUALITY row (DISCERN) to avoid inflating the QUALITY set, but both are available in the same sentence if the reviewer wants them. (5) Engagement means (51 s length, 34,678 views, 3,301 likes, 160 comments per video) and the professional/non-professional DISCERN and PEMAT contrasts are not shares. (6) The three belief categories (48.3% + 37.9% + 6.9% = 93.1%) do not exhaust the 58 videos, and the abstract never states how the residual was coded, nor whether the categories are mutually exclusive - an ambiguity an adjudicator should note. (7) The abstract's conclusion ('TikTok videos endorsing misinformation are popularly viewed') is not supported by any reported view-count comparison between misinformation and non-misinformation videos.

rob.design: Conference abstract (AUA 2023 moderated poster). Hashtag-based TikTok search (#covidvaccine, #malefertility) covering 1 Jan - 31 Dec 2021, unrelated videos excluded, leaving 58 videos; each reviewed by five independent researchers who recorded publication date, length, views, likes, comments, presence of a US-certified medical professional, demographics, scientific article cited, belief held, modified DISCERN and PEMAT scores; SPSS v24. No pre-exclusion count, no inter-rater reliability, no codebook, no country restriction, no protocol registration, and no external fact-check standard reported. Very small denominator (58).
